Chapter 26

The CSRF check we wrote ourselves

Kit 3 blocked a legitimate DELETE and allowed a cross-origin JSON POST. Here is the bug, and the replacement.

By the end of this chapter

Understand CSRF properly, and write a check that is both stricter and looser than the default — in the right directions.

This chapter exists because of a bug report from a curl session, and it is the best kind: the framework was not wrong, it was solving a slightly different problem than the one we had.

What the attack actually is

A browser attaches your cookies to a request for our domain whoever asked for it. So a page on evil.example can contain this:

You visit that page while signed in to the venue. The browser sends the request with your session cookie attached, the venue sees a valid session, and you have just sold a million shares. You clicked nothing on our site. That is cross-site request forgery.

What stops it is the Origin header. The browser sets it to the site the request came *from*, and page JavaScript cannot change it. Same origin — fine. Different origin — refuse.

The bug

While testing the public API by hand, this happened:

A body-less DELETE, authenticated with a Bearer token, from a command-line tool with no origin at all, refused as a cross-site form submission.

Kit's rule is: block a non-GET request when its Content-Type is form-like or absent and the Origin does not match. A DELETE with no body sends no content type. There is nothing an API client can do about this — you cannot ask people to set a content type on a request that has no content.

And there is a second half. A cross-origin POST carrying Content-Type: application/json is *allowed*, because browsers cannot send one without a CORS preflight that our server would decline. That is true today. It also means our safety depends on a browser behaviour rather than on something we check.

Two problems, one root cause

Kit's check keys on content type, because it is defending against HTML forms, which can only send three content types. Our problem is not "is this a form?" — it is "is this request authenticated by a cookie?". CSRF is a cookie attack, start to finish. Key on the credential and both problems disappear at once.

The replacement

Turn Kit's check off, and write the one we actually mean.

trustedOrigins: ['*'] on its own is a serious vulnerability. It is only acceptable here because the hook below runs on every request and is strictly stronger. If you copy the config line without the hook, you have removed your CSRF protection and added nothing.

The rule in one sentence: any state-changing request authenticated by a cookie must carry a matching Origin.

  • GET, HEAD and OPTIONS pass — they must not change anything, and if one of yours does, that is the bug.
  • A Bearer token passes with no origin check. There is no way for evil.example to make your browser attach a token it does not have, so a token-authenticated request cannot be forged this way. That fixes the DELETE.
  • Everything else must match PUBLIC_ORIGIN exactly — including a cross-origin JSON POST, which Kit would have let through. That closes the second half.

The exemption for Bearer tokens is not a convenience. It is a statement about which credential the attack applies to. CSRF works *only* because credentials travel automatically; cookies do, Authorization headers do not.

And the ordering, once more, because it is easy to get backwards:

Refuse the forged request *before* the database round trip that resolves who it claims to be. A rejected request should cost as close to nothing as possible, because rejected requests are the ones that arrive in volume.

Checkpoint

  • You can explain CSRF to somebody without using the word "token"
  • You can explain why a body-less DELETE tripped Kit's content-type rule
  • You can explain why exempting Bearer tokens is safe and exempting a missing Origin is not
  • You know why trustedOrigins: ['*'] is only acceptable alongside the hook
